setupSteps: Clear a strip of floor about 1.5 m long and 1 m wide (est.). Move rugs or slippers that the back foot could catch.
Footwear: barefoot on a non-slip floor or flat trainers. Avoid socks on smooth tiles (slipping risk) and soft, squishy shoes (wobbly).
Support (beginners): stand side-on to a wall, kitchen counter or a sturdy chair placed beside you, close enough to rest your fingertips on it. Do not use a chair with wheels.

Feet: stand tall with feet hip-width apart, toes pointing forward. Picture two railway tracks rather than a tightrope: the feet stay hip-width apart side to side even after you step back (coaching sources; keeps balance).
Hands: on your hips (Harvard Health), lightly on the support, or crossed on the chest. For harder versions, hold dumbbells by your sides.
Posture: chest lifted, shoulders relaxed and down, eyes looking straight ahead at a spot on the wall at eye level.
Back knee cushion (optional): if you will let the knee touch down, place a folded towel or mat where it will land, about one long step behind you.
Clothing: fitted track pants or leggings so you and the camera can see the knee and hip.

steps.part: A. Bodyweight reverse lunge, alternating legs (main version)
steps.title: Brace and stand tall
steps.action: Feet hip-width, weight spread over the whole of both feet. Gently tighten your stomach as if about to cough.
steps.feel: Light firmness around the waist; standing tall.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ear, shoulder, hip and ankle roughly in one vertical line. Front: feet hip-width, toes forward.

steps.part: A. Bodyweight reverse lunge, alternating legs (main version)
steps.title: Shift your weight onto the front (staying) leg
steps.action: Move your weight onto the right foot (if the left leg will step back). Keep the right foot fully planted, heel down.
steps.feel: The right foot and right buttock take your weight.
steps.visualCheck: Front: hips stay level, not swinging out to the side.

steps.part: A. Bodyweight reverse lunge, alternating legs (main version)
steps.title: Step back
steps.action: Take a long, controlled step backwards with the left foot, keeping it hip-width from the right foot. Land softly on the ball of the left foot; the left heel stays lifted (ACE, Harvard).
steps.feel: Most weight stays on the front foot; the back foot is mainly for balance.
steps.visualCheck: Side: step length is long enough that, at the bottom, the front shin is close to vertical. Front: back foot lands in its own "track", not behind the front foot.

steps.part: A. Bodyweight reverse lunge, alternating legs (main version)
steps.title: Lower straight down
steps.action: Bend both knees and lower your body straight down, like an elevator, until the front thigh is about parallel to the floor and the back knee hovers just above the floor (or lightly touches the towel). ACE cues sitting back into the front hip as you lower. Go only as low as you can control (Mayo).
steps.feel: Work in the front thigh and front buttock; a gentle stretch at the front of the back hip.
steps.visualCheck: Side: both knees bent to about 90 degrees; trunk upright or with a slight forward lean; front knee over the middle of the foot. Front: front knee in line with the second toe, not caving in or bowing out (Mayo).

steps.part: A. Bodyweight reverse lunge, alternating legs (main version)
steps.title: Pause at the bottom
steps.action: Hold briefly without resting the knee's weight on the floor.
steps.feel: Steady and balanced; front heel still down.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back knee a few centimetres off the floor, pointing down, not forward.

steps.part: A. Bodyweight reverse lunge, alternating legs (main version)
steps.title: Drive back up
steps.action: Push the front foot firmly into the floor (mostly through the heel and middle of the foot) and stand up, bringing the back foot forward to meet it. ACE cues pulling the front knee slightly back while swinging the back leg forward.
steps.feel: The front buttock and thigh do the work; the back leg only helps a little.
steps.breathing: Breathe out as you rise. Do not hold your breath.
steps.visualCheck: Side: trunk rises without first pitching forward. Front: front knee stays over the toes.

steps.part: A. Bodyweight reverse lunge, alternating legs (main version)
steps.title: Stand tall and reset
steps.action: Return to feet hip-width, fully upright, weight even. Then repeat with the other leg stepping back.
steps.visualCheck: Side: knees straight (not locked hard), hips fully forward, body vertical again.

steps.title: Take the bottom-position stance: one foot forward, one foot about a long step behind, hip-width apart, back heel lifted

steps.title: Lower straight down (2 s) and rise (1–2 s) without moving the feet. ExRx lists the split squat as the easier version of the rear lunge

commonMistakes.title: Front knee caving inward
commonMistakes.text: Front knee caving inward. Why: strains the inside of the knee and means the side-hip muscles are not doing their job. Fix: push the front knee gently out over the second toe; use a shorter range or the supported version until it stays in line.

commonMistakes.title: Stepping onto a tightrope (feet in one line)
commonMistakes.text: Stepping onto a tightrope (feet in one line). Why: makes balance very hard, so you wobble and twist. Fix: keep the feet hip-width apart, like railway tracks, even when you step back.

commonMistakes.title: Step too short, so the front heel lifts and the knee shoots far forward
commonMistakes.text: Step too short, so the front heel lifts and the knee shoots far forward. Why: puts more of the work on the front of the knee and shifts weight to the toes. Fix: step further back; keep the front heel down. Note: the knee travelling a little past the toes is not automatically dangerous (Fry et al. 2003 showed that blocking forward knee travel in a squat shifts load to the hips and lower back), but for beginners the front heel must stay down.

commonMistakes.title: Slamming the back knee into the floor
commonMistakes.text: Slamming the back knee into the floor. Why: painful on the kneecap, noisy for neighbours, and means the lowering is uncontrolled. Fix: lower in 2 seconds; stop a few centimetres above the floor or touch a folded towel lightly.

commonMistakes.title: Leaning far forward with a rounded back, or leaning back
commonMistakes.text: Leaning far forward with a rounded back, or leaning back. Why: rounding loads the lower back (the UK osteoporosis consensus advises avoiding loaded forward bending); leaning back arches it. Fix: chest proud, eyes ahead; a slight forward lean from the hips with a flat back is fine.

commonMistakes.title: Pushing off the back foot to stand up
commonMistakes.text: Pushing off the back foot to stand up. Why: the back leg and momentum do the work, and the front leg gets less training. Fix: think "front heel drives me up"; pause at the bottom first.

commonMistakes.title: Rushing and bouncing
commonMistakes.text: Rushing and bouncing. Why: less control, more wobble and knee strain. Fix: 1 s step, 2 s down, 1 s pause, 1–2 s up.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: breath-holding (Valsalva) raises blood pressure more than breathing during effort (1992 study of novice lifters, BJSM). Fix: breathe in on the way down, out on the way up.

safetyNotes: Knee problems (kneecap pain, osteoarthritis, after knee injury): the reverse lunge is usually better tolerated than the forward lunge (lower patellofemoral load in the 2021 lab study), but use a shorter step-down range, keep the front heel down, and stop if knee pain rises. Several clinic sources advise people with knee arthritis to avoid deep lunges (front knee past 90°).

Lower back problems: keep the trunk upright and the stomach lightly braced; avoid rounding forward; start with the split squat. The backward lunge works the back muscles more than the forward lunge (Song and Yoo 2021), which is fine for most people but may be noticed during a flare.
Balance problems, dizziness, older adults, osteoporosis: always use a wall or chair for support; the main risk is a fall, not the movement itself.

Pregnancy: balance changes as pregnancy progresses, and ACOG advises avoiding activities with a high fall risk; use support. NHS pelvic girdle pain leaflets advise reducing movements that take one leg away from the other, so skip lunges if you have pelvic girdle (pubic or sacroiliac) pain.
Postpartum: start with pelvic floor exercises; add supported, shallow lunges once cleared and free of heaviness, leaking or pain.
High blood pressure and heart disease: breathe continuously, keep effort moderate, no straining.
Recent hip, knee, ankle or spine surgery: only with your surgeon's or physiotherapist's approval.
